sections.title: Executive summary
sections.text: Advertising inefficiency is the best-supported explanation for the deterioration, while ad fatigue remains a plausible competing mechanism. The available aggregate evidence does not distinguish them or establish a definitive cause. Delivery delays are a possible but weakly supported contributor. Checkout failure and stockout are not supported by the supplied records; lower sessions, orders, and revenue do not by themselves identify their cause.

sections.title: Observed evidence
sections.text:
Campaign performance versus baseline and peers: 5 campaign(s) analysed over 30 h ending 2026-10-05T12:00:00.000Z: CTR 0.33%, spend £625.83, 10 attributed orders, CPA £62.58, ROAS 1.64. Versus baseline: CTR -82.5%, hourly spend +27.2%, hourly attributed orders -56.5%. Observations are simulated ad-platform records; frequency and CTR describe exposure and response, not intent.

Revenue, orders and conversion versus baseline: Over 30 h ending 2026-10-05T12:00:00.000Z: 20 orders, net revenue £1944.54, 787 sessions, conversion 2.54%. Baseline (30 h): hourly revenue -46.9% change, hourly orders -37.5%, hourly sessions -46.9%. Decomposition: sessions share 0.998, conversion share -0.257, AOV share 0.259 of the revenue change. Values are simulated business records; this describes what changed, not why.

Sessions, conversion and checkout failures: 787 sessions and 20 orders over 30 h ending 2026-10-05T12:00:00.000Z (conversion 2.54%); 0 checkout failures (0.00% of sessions). Baseline: conversion 2.16% (+17.7% change), failures per hour n/a change, sessions per hour -46.9% change. Simulated storefront records; device and channel slices join orders to their canonical session.

Inventory levels, depletion and demand velocity: 17 product(s) observed to 2026-10-05T12:00:00.000Z: 0 at zero available units, 0 projected to run out within 72 h at current velocity, 10 units depleted in the 30 h window, 0 out-of-stock checkout failures. No product is currently out of stock. Simulated inventory records derived from canonical inventory.level_changed events.

Review volume, low ratings and delivery complaints: 1 reviews over 30 h ending 2026-10-05T12:00:00.000Z: 0 rated ≤2 (0.0%), average rating 4.00, 1 mention delivery terms. Most low-rated products: Nike Vomero 18 (0/1). Simulated review records; delivery mentions are a keyword heuristic.

Delivery promise cohort and delayed orders: Cohort of 44 promises due in the 30 h ending 2026-10-05T12:00:00.000Z: 5 not delivered by promise (late rate 11.4%). Baseline late rate 0.0% on 13 promises (n/a change). 3 order(s) received a delayed status (average recorded delay 1919 min), 0 lost; 5 shipped order(s) are past promise with no delivered or lost event at the cutoff. Simulated fulfilment records; cohort membership is by promise due date, so immature promises never read as healthy.

sections.title: Competing explanations
sections.text:
ad inefficiency (moderate): Reduced click and attributed-order outcomes alongside higher hourly spend support deteriorating advertising efficiency. The evidence does not identify whether campaign settings, delivery, audience response, or attribution changes drove the pattern.

ad fatigue (moderate): Higher observed frequency alongside lower CTR is consistent with ad fatigue, but the same aggregate observations cannot distinguish fatigue from changes in creative, targeting, placement, delivery, or measurement.

delivery delays (weak): Late deliveries and a past-promise backlog were observed, so delivery experiences could be a contributing factor. No customer, product, or campaign linkage establishes that they explain the advertising deterioration; storefront conversion did not decline, and feedback evidence is sparse.

sections.title: Causal challenges and uncertainty
sections.text:
Higher observed frequency alongside lower CTR is consistent with ad fatigue, but does not show that repeated exposure caused the decline. Campaign mix, creative, targeting, delivery, or measurement changes remain alternatives.
Chronology: Higher frequency and lower CTR are observed in the same incident window; the supplied evidence does not establish which changed first.
Controls: The advertising analysis compares affected campaigns with a baseline, not with matched unaffected audiences or campaigns.
Confounders: Targeting, creative, placement, bid, or platform delivery changes could lower CTR.; The affected campaigns span paid search and paid social, which may have different exposure dynamics.
Could be weakened by: Compare matched audience and creative groups with different exposure histories; no relationship between exposure and response would weaken the fatigue hypothesis.; Check whether comparable low-frequency groups show a similar CTR decline; an equal decline would weaken the repeated-exposure mechanism.
